summary.text: VSEPR theory is a model used in chemistry to predict the geometry of individual molecules from the number of electron pairs around their central atoms.
Its premise is that the valence electron pairs around an atom repel each other, so the predicted geometry is the one with as little repulsion as possible.
It treats the repulsion by a lone pair as greater than that by a bonding pair, which helps explain deviations from idealised geometries.

facts.label: Refined in
facts.value: 1957, by Gillespie and Nyholm in London

facts.label: Classroom demo
facts.value: Five tied balloons adopt the PCl₅ shape

items.prompt: Three electron groups surround a central atom. Where do they sit to repel one another as little as possible?

options.label: In a straight line, one at each end and one between
At the corners of an equilateral triangle around the atom
At the corners of a square around the atom
Clustered together on one side of the atom

items.explain: With three electron pairs, repulsion is minimized by placing them at the vertices of an equilateral triangle centered on the atom.

items.prompt: A central atom is joined to one atom by a double bond and to two other atoms by single bonds, with no lone pairs. How many bonding groups does VSEPR count around it?

options.label: Two
Four
Three
Five

items.explain: VSEPR theory treats a double or triple bond as a single bonding group, so the three attached atoms give three groups.

items.prompt: Why does VSEPR theory treat a lone pair as pushing harder on its neighbours than a shared pair does?

options.label: A lone pair carries a larger charge than a shared pair
A shared pair is pinned in place by the covalent bond
A lone pair contains more electrons than a shared pair
A lone pair is held close to its own positively charged nucleus

items.explain: A bonding pair lies further from the central atom, while a lone pair is held close to its nucleus, so repulsion by the lone pair is viewed as greater.

items.prompt: Why do inflated balloons tied together make a handy demonstration of electron-pair geometry?

options.label: They gain a slight surface charge and so spread out like electron pairs
Their rubber forms bonds in the same pattern as phosphorus
The air inside them pushes toward the corners of a cube
They are made of the same material as an electron pair

items.explain: Handling gives balloons a slight electrostatic charge, so tied together they adopt roughly the same geometries as the corresponding number of electron pairs.

items.prompt: In a molecule with five electron pairs, a lone pair can take a position with three close neighbours or one with only two. Where does it tend to go?

options.label: With three close neighbours, so the others feel less repulsion
Anywhere, since all positions feel the same repulsion
The position with two close neighbours, where it feels less repulsion
Whichever position lies closest to the nucleus

items.explain: Axial positions have more close neighbours at 90° and so more repulsion; lone pairs tend to occupy the equatorial positions.

items.prompt: Which pairing of electron pairs repels most strongly in VSEPR theory?

options.label: Two lone pairs
A lone pair and a bonding pair
Two bonding pairs
All three repel equally

items.explain: Lone pair–lone pair repulsions are considered stronger than lone pair–bonding pair repulsions, which are stronger than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsions.
